### The Private Provision of Public Services (AER, 2026)

Nearly 100,000 Medicaid enrollees were **randomly assigned** between a publicly operated
fee-for-service system and private managed care. Points show the effect of managed care on
annual spending by category; hover for the 95% confidence interval.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(plotly)
d <- read.csv("data/result_aer2026.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
d$outcome <- factor(d$outcome, levels = rev(d$outcome))
plot_ly(d, y = ~outcome, x = ~estimate, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
        marker = list(color = "#00356B", size = 9),
        error_x = list(type = "data", symmetric = FALSE,
                       array = ~(ci_high - estimate),
                       arrayminus = ~(estimate - ci_low),
                       color = "#00356B"),
        hovertemplate = ~paste0(outcome, ": ", estimate,
                                "% [", ci_low, ", ", ci_high, "]<extra></extra>")) |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Effect of managed care on spending (%)", zeroline = TRUE),
         yaxis = list(title = ""), margin = list(l = 10)) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

**Takeaway:** managed care lowered total spending (−5.6%), driven almost entirely by
**pharmacy** management (−18%). Outpatient spending fell modestly and inpatient was
essentially unchanged. Yet privatizing medical benefits was associated with **lower measured
quality and consumer satisfaction** — the savings did not come free.
[Read the paper →](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20230541)

*95% confidence intervals are derived from the standard errors reported in NBER WP30390 and are pending final verification against the published tables.*
:::
